section.title: The Promise of Restoration
section.sectionRationale: Still confined in the courtyard of the guard as the siege presses in, Jeremiah receives a second word of hope, an invitation to call on God and be shown great and unsearchable things. What follows is a promise of healing for the devastated city, and, at its center, the Righteous Branch of David who will execute justice and righteousness and bear the name The LORD Our Righteousness.
section.thesis: Even from a prison cell in a doomed city, God's covenant faithfulness is as fixed as the cycle of day and night, guaranteeing not only the physical rebuilding of Jerusalem but the coming of a righteous Davidic king in whom God's own righteousness becomes His people's name and hope.
section.frameNote: Five scenes: God's invitation to call and be shown unsearchable things; the promise of healing, joy, and forgiveness for the ruined city; the Righteous Branch of David and the name The LORD Our Righteousness; God's covenant with David and the Levites made as unbreakable as day and night; and the assurance that Israel's descendants will never be finally rejected.

units.label: Call to Me, and I will answer

verses.text: While Jeremiah was still confined in the courtyard of the guard, the word of the LORD came to him a second time:
“Thus says the LORD who made the earth, the LORD who formed it and established it, the LORD is His name:
Call to Me, and I will answer and show you great and unsearchable things you do not know.
For this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says about the houses of this city and the palaces of the kings of Judah that have been torn down for defense against the siege ramps and the sword:

The Chaldeans are coming to fight and to fill those places with the corpses of the men I will strike down in My anger and in My wrath. I have hidden My face from this city because of all its wickedness.

units.label: Healing and joy for the ruined city

verses.text: Nevertheless, I will bring to it health and healing, and I will heal its people and reveal to them the abundance of peace and truth.
I will restore Judah and Israel from captivity and will rebuild them as in former times.
And I will cleanse them from all the iniquity they have committed against Me, and will forgive all their sins of rebellion against Me.

So this city will bring Me renown, joy, praise, and glory before all the nations of the earth, who will hear of all the good I do for it. They will tremble in awe because of all the goodness and prosperity that I will provide for it.

This is what the LORD says: In this place you say is a wasteland without man or beast, in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem that are deserted, inhabited by neither man nor beast, there will be heard again

the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom, and the voices of those bringing thank offerings into the house of the LORD, saying: 
‘Give thanks to the LORD of Hosts, for the LORD is good; 
His loving devotion endures forever.’ 
For I will restore the land from captivity as in former times, says the LORD.
This is what the LORD of Hosts says: In this desolate place, without man or beast, and in all its cities, there will once more be pastures for shepherds to rest their flocks.

In the cities of the hill country, the foothills, and the Negev, in the land of Benjamin and the cities surrounding Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, the flocks will again pass under the hands of the one who counts them, says the LORD.

units.label: The Righteous Branch, The LORD Our Righteousness
units.note: a king and a priesthood secured forever

verses.text: Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will fulfill the gracious promise that I have spoken to the house of Israel and the house of Judah.
In those days and at that time I will cause to sprout for David a righteous {{tsemach|Branch}}, and He will administer justice and righteousness in the land.
In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell securely, and this is the name by which it will be called: {{yahwehTsidqenu|The LORD Our Righteousness}}.
For this is what the LORD says: David will never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel,
nor will the priests who are Levites ever fail to have a man before Me to offer burnt offerings, to burn grain offerings, and to present sacrifices.”

units.label: A covenant as fixed as day and night
units.note: as sure as the sun and stars

verses.text: And the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:
“This is what the LORD says: If you can break My {{beritYom|covenant}} with the day and My covenant with the night, so that day and night cease to occupy their appointed time,
then My covenant may also be broken with David My servant and with My ministers the Levites who are priests, so that David will not have a son to reign on his throne.
As the hosts of heaven cannot be counted and as the sand on the seashore cannot be measured, so too will I multiply the descendants of My servant David and the Levites who minister before Me.”
Moreover, the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah:
“Have you not noticed what these people are saying: ‘The LORD has rejected the two families He had chosen’? So they despise My people and no longer regard them as a nation.
This is what the LORD says: If I have not established My covenant with the day and the night and the fixed order of heaven and earth,

then I would also reject the descendants of Jacob and of My servant David, so as not to take from his descendants rulers over the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For I will restore them from captivity and will have compassion on them.”

tsemach.gloss: A branch or sprout, growth out of what seems dead. The righteous Tsemach that God causes to sprout for David is a Davidic king raised up in a moment when David's dynasty appeared finished; Zechariah later uses the same term of the same coming figure, Zechariah 3:8, 6:12.

yahwehTsidqenu.gloss: The LORD Our Righteousness, the name given to Jerusalem and, in Jeremiah 23:6, to the Righteous Branch Himself. It declares that the city's security and the people's standing before God rest entirely on a righteousness that is not their own but the LORD's, given to them.

beritYom.gloss: The covenant with the day and the night, God's fixed ordering of creation's rhythm. God stakes His covenant with David and the Levites on the same unbreakable reliability as the daily rising of the sun, an oath as certain as creation itself.

basic.context: Still imprisoned as Jerusalem's siege continues, Jeremiah receives a second word from God, an invitation to call on Him and be shown great and unsearchable things. The chapter promises healing and rebuilding for the devastated city, and at its center announces a righteous Branch of David who will bring true justice, a king under whom the city itself will be renamed The LORD Our Righteousness.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real promise to a real, defeated nation, grounded in God's own unbreakable faithfulness rather than in Judah's merit, since the surrounding chapters have already shown how thoroughly Judah has broken covenant. The righteous Branch names a coming, specific individual, not merely a general improvement in national fortunes, as the New Testament's application to Christ confirms.
basic.originalLanguages: God promises to cause a tsemach, a righteous Branch, to sprout for David out of a dynasty that seemed finished, and under Him Jerusalem will be called by the name yahwehTsidqenu, the LORD Our Righteousness. This whole promise rests on the beritYom, God's covenant with the day and the night, as unbreakable as creation's own rhythm.
basic.typology: The righteous Branch who administers justice and righteousness, and under whom the city is renamed The LORD Our Righteousness, anticipates Christ, who is Himself made our righteousness before God, 1 Corinthians 1:30. The everlasting Davidic throne, secured by a covenant as sure as day and night, anticipates the eternal reign of Christ, the true and final Son of David, Luke 1:32-33.
basic.christ: Jesus is the righteous Branch this chapter promises, the Son of David who brings true justice and righteousness. Paul teaches that Christ Himself has become our righteousness, 1 Corinthians 1:30, fulfilling the very name given to the city here, The LORD Our Righteousness, so that believers, not just Jerusalem, now bear that righteousness as their own standing before God.
basic.god: God is the one who hides His face in righteous judgment yet promises health, healing, and full forgiveness on the other side of that judgment. His covenant faithfulness to David and to His people is grounded not in their performance but in His own unchangeable character, as fixed and reliable as the sun's rising and the stars' courses.
basic.crossReferences: Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12 take up the same title, the Branch, for the same coming Davidic figure. 1 Corinthians 1:30 declares that Christ Himself has become our righteousness, wisdom, sanctification, and redemption. Luke 1:32-33 promises Jesus an eternal throne on David's line, fulfilling the everlasting dynasty promised here. Hebrews 7:23-25 shows Christ's own priesthood permanently securing what the Levitical priesthood, promised here to continue, could only foreshadow.
basic.oneStory: From a prison cell in a city about to fall, God promises not only that Jerusalem will be rebuilt but that a righteous Branch of David will come, under whom His people will be known by His own righteousness. That promise is fulfilled in Christ, the eternal Son of David who is Himself our righteousness and whose priesthood secures forever what Levi's could only foreshadow.

context.literary:
Chapter 33 opens by saying the word came 'a second time', which ties it to chapter 32 and tells us the prison scene has not changed. It then proceeds as a chain of short oracles, each opened by a fresh 'This is what the LORD says' or 'the word of the LORD came', in verses 2, 10, 12, 14, 19 and 23. The effect is a staircase. Each step takes a despairing sentence that the people are saying and answers it. The houses torn down for defence, verse 4, are answered by rebuilding. The land called a wasteland 'without man or beast', verse 10, is answered by wedding songs and shepherds, verses 10 to 13. The fear that the throne and the priesthood have ended, verses 17 and 18, is answered by a covenant stronger than the calendar, verses 19 to 22. And the people's own verdict, 'The LORD has rejected the two families He had chosen', verse 24, is answered by an oath on the order of creation, verses 25 and 26.

Inside this staircase the middle section is the centre of gravity. Verses 14 to 16 are a compressed echo of Jeremiah 23:5 to 6, the earlier Branch oracle, with one notable change that we will return to: the name 'The LORD Our Righteousness' is given to the city in 33:16 but to the king in 23:6. The surrounding oracles are full of reversals of earlier judgments. The 'sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom' in verse 11 are exactly the sounds the LORD said he would silence in Jeremiah 7:34, 16:9 and 25:10. This is a deliberate undoing of the book's own sentences of doom.

The prayer invitation of verse 3 stands apart at the head of the chapter. 'Call to Me, and I will answer' is not a general maxim dropped in passing. It is the door into the whole chapter: the prophet is told to ask, and what follows is the answer.
context.historical:
The setting is the same confinement as chapter 32, the courtyard of the guard, in the final year of the siege around 587 BC. Verse 4 describes a detail of the city's defence: the houses and the palaces of the kings have been 'torn down for defense against the siege ramps'. When an attacker's ramp rose against a wall, defenders pulled down nearby buildings to get stone and timber to strengthen it. Jerusalem is dismantling its own homes to hold out a little longer. The 'corpses' of verse 5 and the 'wasteland without man or beast' of verse 10 are not predictions from a distance. They describe what Jeremiah can already see and smell.

The two promises that lie at the heart of the chapter were the two institutions that seemed about to die. The Davidic king had been promised an everlasting house, 2 Samuel 7:16, and Psalm 89:34 to 37 sets that promise next to the sun and moon. Yet Zedekiah, the last king, was about to lose his sons and his eyes, 2 Kings 25:7. The priesthood stood on God's covenant with Levi, Malachi 2:4 to 5, and with Aaron's grandson Phinehas, a 'covenant of permanent priesthood', Numbers 25:13, and the temple was about to burn. The hearers had every reason to say that both were ended. Verse 24 records that they did.

The word 'Chaldeans' in verses 4 and 5 is the BSB's rendering for the Babylonians, and the BSB note observes that verse 5 can be read in more than one way, since the Hebrew can also be understood as 'They are coming to fight the Chaldeans'. Either reading leaves the siege and its consequences in place, and the sense of the verse remains that the defences will be filled with the dead.

The geography of verse 13 lists the regions where flocks will be counted again: the hill country, the foothills (the Shephelah, according to the BSB note), the Negev, Benjamin and the cities around Jerusalem. It is the same list as the roll call of the land that would be bought and sold again in Jeremiah 32:44, and it covers the whole territory of the kingdom. The promise is not for one city. It is for the entire land that was about to be emptied.
context.canonical:
The chapter belongs with a family of texts about a coming Davidic shoot. Jeremiah 23:5 to 6 is its immediate parent, and Isaiah 4:2 speaks of 'the Branch of the LORD' in the day of restoration. Zechariah then takes the word as a title, 'My servant, the Branch', Zechariah 3:8, and 'a man whose name is the Branch', Zechariah 6:12. It is worth saying that Isaiah 11:1 speaks of a shoot from the stump of Jesse using other Hebrew words, so the family is related by theme and not by one word alone. Psalm 132:17 uses the same verb of sprouting for David's horn, 'There I will make a horn grow for David', and Luke 1:69 echoes it when Zechariah sings of 'a horn of salvation' raised up in David's house.

The covenant with day and night, verses 20 and 25, belongs to the creation-covenant thread running through Genesis 8:22 and Jeremiah 31:35 to 37, where the same fixed order of sun, moon and stars is the pledge that Israel will never cease to be a nation. The priestly and Levitical promise in verse 18 links to Numbers 25:12 and 13 and Malachi 2:4 to 5, and in Isaiah 66:21 the LORD says he will take priests and Levites even from the nations.

In the New Testament the chapter's Branch is read in Luke 1:32 to 33, 69 and 78, in Romans 15:12, and in Revelation 22:16, where Jesus calls himself 'the Root and the Offspring of David'. The name of the city is applied to believers in 1 Corinthians 1:30, where Christ has become 'our righteousness'. The priestly promise is carried by Hebrews 7:23 to 25 and 10:11 to 14, and by 1 Peter 2:9 and Revelation 5:10, where the whole people of God are 'a royal priesthood' and 'priests to serve our God'. Isaiah 62:4 and Ezekiel 48:35 supply parallels to the renaming of Jerusalem.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Jeremiah's task in this chapter is to put into words what no one in the besieged city could say with a straight face. He has been promised a future, and he has to say it aloud while the walls are failing. He answers a particular despair, the conviction recorded in verse 24 that the LORD has thrown away both families he once chose. The author therefore moves from quoting the people's despair to quoting the LORD's covenant, and he lets the second outweigh the first.

The first hearers are meant to learn that God's promises are not hostages to their circumstances or their record. Verse 5 does not hide the cause of the siege, 'all its wickedness', and the cleansing of verse 8 is stated as God's own act. The people are not asked to earn the restoration. They are asked to believe that the same LORD who 'made the earth' and 'formed it', verse 2, is the one who has pledged himself.

The Branch oracle is placed at the centre to give them a person to look to. Judah's collapse has been a collapse of leaders, and Jeremiah has already condemned the kings of Judah. Here he says that a king is coming who will do what they failed to do: 'administer justice and righteousness in the land', verse 15. Jeremiah means the hearers to hold on to the line of David as a promise about someone, not merely about an institution, and to let that expectation shape the way they live through the exile.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records God's promises to a particular people in a particular crisis and describes what he will do for Jerusalem, Judah and the lines of David and Levi. It does not command any particular behaviour except that it invites prayer, verse 3. Readers should not treat the promise of rebuilt cities or bustling pastures as an assurance that any modern city or business will be restored, and the promise of 'health and healing' in verse 6 is not a pledge of medical healing for each believer. It concerns the healing of a wounded people and a ruined city.

What carries over is what the New Testament carries over. The invitation to call on God and receive answers is repeated in Jesus' own teaching, and the New Testament applies the Branch promise to Christ. Believers are invited to see, in the gift of righteousness, the name given to the city, and in the priestly promise, their own calling as priests, 1 Peter 2:9. The principle that God's covenant is more reliable than the calendar encourages believers, though it is a promise to the covenant community, and it is claimed in Christ, not in general. A reader who hears 'Call to Me' as a formula for getting great things from God has misread it: the great things the LORD names here are the restoration of a people and the coming of a king.

debates.question: Does the promise that David will never lack a man to sit on the throne, verse 17, require an unbroken line of literal Davidic kings on an earthly throne?

views.label: Fulfilled in Christ's eternal reign, not a continuous earthly dynasty
views.case: The Davidic throne was in fact vacant for centuries after the exile; the New Testament resolves this by identifying Jesus, the final Son of David, as the one who reigns forever, Luke 1:32-33, so the promise is kept in Him rather than through an unbroken succession of literal kings.

views.label: A promise whose ultimate guarantee is a still-future, visible Davidic reign
views.case: Some hold the promise anticipates a future, earthly reign of the Davidic Messiah still to come, in addition to His present spiritual reign, since the language of verse 16 speaks of Jerusalem dwelling securely in terms not yet fully realized.

debates.bearing: Both views agree the promise is secured in Christ, the true Son of David; they differ chiefly on whether its fullest, visible realization is entirely present now or still partly future, a question that does not diminish the certainty of the promise itself.

debates.question: How should we read the promise that Levitical priests will always offer sacrifices, verse 18?

views.label: Fulfilled in Christ and his people
views.case: Hebrews 7:23 to 25 says Christ has a permanent priesthood because he lives forever, and Hebrews 10:11 to 14 says his one sacrifice has done what repeated sacrifices could not. 1 Peter 2:9 and Revelation 5:10 call the whole people of God priests. Isaiah 66:21 already pictured priests and Levites drawn from the nations, which suggests the promise was always larger than one tribe.

views.label: A literal future priesthood and sacrifice
views.case: Some read verse 18 together with the temple vision of Ezekiel 40 to 48 as describing a literal priesthood and offerings in a restored age. They argue the promise is stated with the same weight as the Davidic one, and that Scripture does not say the Levites are replaced.

debates.bearing: The disagreement is about how the New Testament reads the Old Testament's sacrificial system, and Christians differ. Both sides agree that the promise stands on God's covenant, and that no priest or offering can stand before God apart from the sacrifice of Christ.

debates.question: Why are verses 14 to 26 missing from the Septuagint, and does that affect how we read them?

views.label: Part of Jeremiah's original message, shortened in the Greek tradition
views.case: The Greek translation of Jeremiah is notably shorter than the Hebrew and omits several passages. The verses are present in the Hebrew text that the Reformation-era and later church has received, and they echo Jeremiah 23:5 to 6 and 31:35 to 37 so closely in thought that they read as Jeremiah's own development.

views.label: A later addition by editors
views.case: Others suggest that the verses were added after the Greek translation was made, in the circles that preserved Jeremiah's words. They note that the promise of priests and Levites reads differently from other parts of the book, and that the Greek lacks any such passage.

debates.bearing: The text of Jeremiah in the Hebrew Bible stands as Scripture whichever way the history of the text is explained, and the New Testament's use of the Branch theme does not depend on this chapter alone. The question affects how we reconstruct how the book grew, not what the church receives as the word of God.

study.originalLanguages:
The word translated 'health' in verse 6 is arukhah, which in Hebrew means the new flesh that grows over a wound as it closes. It is a surgeon's image, and it recurs in Jeremiah 8:22, 'Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?', and 30:17, 'I will restore your health and heal your wounds'. In chapter 8 the question was asked in grief, and in chapter 33 it is answered. The verse then adds a second verb, heal, so that the city is both bandaged and healed, and the result is 'peace and truth', which one might render 'security and reliability'.

The verb 'cause to sprout' in verse 15 is the verb behind the noun 'Branch'. It is the same verb Psalm 132:17 uses of David's horn growing, and the root is the ordinary Hebrew for plants coming up from the ground. The thought is of life coming from a root that looked dead, a family tree that has been cut down to the stump. The Septuagint translators rendered this noun by a Greek word meaning a rising, as of sun or star, and many scholars note that Luke 1:78 uses the related noun for 'the Dawn' that visits us from on high. That is a link that should be held lightly, since the Greek translators were interpreting, but it shows how the first readers of the Branch promise heard in it the language of light.

The phrase that the Branch will 'administer justice and righteousness', verse 15, joins mishpat and tsedaqah, the pair that describes God's own character in many texts and is the standard of the king in Psalm 72:1 to 2. The name given to the city in verse 16, in the BSB's footnote simply 'YHWH Tsidqenu', stands in a quiet play with the name of the last king, Zedekiah, which means 'my righteousness is the LORD'. In the last days of the dynasty, the last king bore a name that the Branch will make true. The word tsedaqah is therefore not an abstract idea in this chapter. It is a name, and a name given to a place and its people.

The refrain of verse 11, 'Give thanks to the LORD of Hosts, for the LORD is good; His loving devotion endures forever', contains chesed, the covenant love of God. The sentence is a recognised liturgy, found in Psalm 136:1, 2 Chronicles 5:13 and Ezra 3:11, where it was sung when the new temple's foundation was laid. The promise is that the song of the temple, silenced in the exile, will be sung again. Finally the BSB note on verse 7 observes that 'restore from captivity' can also be read 'restore the fortunes of Judah and Israel', and the same alternative appears in verses 11 and 26. The Hebrew phrase can mean either, and the sense moves between a return from exile and a general reversal of ruin.

A note on verse 2 is also worth making. The BSB note says its reading 'who made the earth' follows the Septuagint, while the Hebrew has 'who made it'. In the Hebrew the pronoun 'it' has no stated antecedent, and some readers take it to refer to the plan about to be announced, so that the LORD is the one who made the coming restoration, formed it and set it up. Either way, the verse grounds the promise in the maker's power.

typology.type: The righteous Branch of David, Jeremiah 33:15
typology.fulfillment: The Branch is the promised king who rises from a family that seemed cut off. Zechariah takes the word as a title, Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12, and the New Testament sees it in Jesus, 'the Root and the Offspring of David', Revelation 22:16, who is raised up to David's throne, Luke 1:32 and 33. The escalation is that this Branch not only rules justly but also gives his people his own righteousness, 1 Corinthians 1:30. The type is partial in that Davidic kings could be the Branch's forerunners only by failing and being corrected, as the previous chapters have shown.

typology.type: The city named The LORD Our Righteousness, Jeremiah 33:16
typology.fulfillment: Jerusalem receives a name that states where its righteousness comes from. Paul says Christ has become for us 'righteousness', 1 Corinthians 1:30, and that God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God', 2 Corinthians 5:21. Where the city bears the name, the redeemed people in Christ bear the reality, and Revelation 21:2 pictures the holy city as a bride made ready. The type falls short because a city's name is a promise, while Christ's righteousness is a possession credited now.

typology.type: The priests who never lack a man to offer sacrifices, Jeremiah 33:18
typology.fulfillment: The Levitical office is the pattern of mediation between God and his people. Hebrews says that a priesthood that death interrupts is replaced by one that never ends, 'But because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood', Hebrews 7:24, and that he has offered 'one sacrifice for sins' for all time, Hebrews 10:12. The type is inadequate in that Levitical sacrifices 'can never take away sins', Hebrews 10:11. Peter extends the priestly calling to all believers, 1 Peter 2:9, so that the promise of priests widens rather than disappears.

typology.type: The covenant with day and night, Jeremiah 33:20
typology.fulfillment: The fixed order of the heavens is held up as a pledge that God's covenant with David and Levi cannot fail, and Psalm 89:36 and 37 uses the same comparison, the throne endures 'like the sun'. The rising of the sun is itself a figure of Christ in Luke 1:78. Paul's argument in Romans 11:28 and 29, that 'God's gifts and His call are irrevocable', is the New Testament application of the same reasoning to Israel. The type does not mean that creation's order is itself the covenant. It serves as a visible sign that the covenant is as unbreakable as the things God has made.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by promise more directly than most of Jeremiah. The Branch of verse 15 is a person who will arise for David, will 'administer justice and righteousness', and under whom 'Judah will be saved'. The verb behind 'saved' in verse 16 is the root from which the name Joshua, in Greek Jesus, comes, which is why Matthew can say that the child will be called Jesus because he will save his people from their sins, a connection suggested by the root's meaning rather than proved by this verse alone. The Gospels begin by calling Jesus 'the son of David', Matthew 1:1, and Paul says the Root of Jesse 'will arise to rule over the Gentiles', Romans 15:12. The place where Jeremiah promised a righteous king is the place where the Gospel writers begin.

Look at how the chapter joins two roles that Israel kept apart. Verses 17 and 18 promise a king and priests, and Zechariah 6:13 sees them in one man: 'He will be a priest on His throne'. Jeremiah 30:21 has also said that the ruler 'will approach Me, for who would dare on his own to approach Me?' A king who is also the one permitted to draw near is a priest-king, and that is how Hebrews 4:14 to 16 describes Jesus, a great high priest who has passed through the heavens and who invites us to the throne of grace. The same man who sits at the right hand of the Majesty, Hebrews 8:1, intercedes for those he rules, Romans 8:34. Here the two promises, throne and altar, find a single home.

The renaming of the city carries a further thought. The name 'The LORD Our Righteousness' asserts that the city is righteous because of what God gives it. This is the shape of the gospel. Paul says that God has presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice 'to demonstrate His righteousness', so that he might be 'just and the one who justifies', Romans 3:25 and 26. The righteousness is not generated by the people. It comes from the LORD and is credited to them, and Paul states the exchange sharply in 2 Corinthians 5:21. The cleansing and forgiveness of verse 8, 'I will cleanse them from all the iniquity... and will forgive all their sins', is the Old Testament form of the same exchange.

Care is needed so that the text is not forced. Jeremiah does not name Jesus, and the first hearers heard a promise about a coming king in David's line and about a restored people. The New Testament's claim is that Jesus is the one in whom the promise comes true, and the question of what in the chapter is still future, such as the visible security of Jerusalem in verse 16, belongs to the debates above. What is clear is that the throne promised to David, the priesthood promised to Levi and the righteousness promised to the city are all things the New Testament says Christ provides.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who answers prayer with more than was asked. 'Call to Me, and I will answer and show you great and unsearchable things you do not know', verse 3. He is the maker of the earth, verse 2, who sets the courses of day and night, verses 20 and 25, and the same God is the one who makes promises to a king and a priesthood. His power over creation is offered as the ground of his trustworthiness toward his people. If the sun rises on time, so does his word.

The chapter does not hide his anger. Verse 5 says, 'I have hidden My face from this city because of all its wickedness', which draws on the warning of Deuteronomy 31:17 and 18 that he would hide his face from a people who turned to other gods. The hiding of the face is the opposite of the blessing of his face shining on them. Yet the sentence that follows begins with 'Nevertheless'. Anger is real but it is not the last word, and the restoration that follows is entirely a work of his initiative: 'I will bring', 'I will heal', 'I will cleanse', 'I will forgive', 'I will restore'. The verbs of the whole chapter are in his mouth.

The picture of his glory in verse 9 is unusual. The restored city will bring him 'renown, joy, praise, and glory before all the nations', and the nations will tremble 'because of all the goodness and prosperity that I will provide for it'. God's mercy toward Judah has an audience beyond Judah. His faithfulness to a small, failed people is a display for the world of what kind of God he is, and it opens a path for the nations to fear him. The covenant with David and with Levi is not only for their sake but for the sake of his name.

His faithfulness is grounded in himself, not in his people. When they say he has rejected the two families, verse 24, he does not cite their repentance. He cites creation, verses 25 and 26, as a pledge made visible every morning. That is how Numbers 23:19 can say that God does not lie or change his mind, and how Romans 11:1 and 2 can say that God did not reject his people. This should shape our worship in two ways. First, we praise the one who keeps promises we have not deserved, and sing, as verse 11 says the restored people will, 'His loving devotion endures forever'. Second, we learn that confidence in God is not confidence in our consistency, and that prayer, verse 3, is the proper response to promises as large as these.

crossReferences.note: The earlier form of the Branch promise, with the same king, the same justice and righteousness and the same name. In 23:6 the name belongs to the king; in 33:16 it belongs to the city. The shift shows that what the Branch is, his people become, so the two passages should be read as one promise told twice.

The sun, moon and stars are named here as the fixed order that guarantees Israel's survival as a nation, and the measuring of the heavens is the image of the impossible. Jeremiah 33:20 to 26 reuses the argument for the Davidic and Levitical lines, so the two chapters answer the same fear.

The question about the health of the people, 'Is there no balm in Gilead?', is asked in grief. Jeremiah 33:6 answers it with the same word for health and with a promise to heal. Reading them together shows that the book is bringing its own sorrows to resolution.

The silencing of the bride and bridegroom's voices is announced here as a sign of coming ruin. Jeremiah 33:11 gives the same voices back, along with the thanksgiving song, so the reversal is a point-for-point answer to the sentence.

Moses warned that God would hide his face from a people who turned to other gods. Jeremiah 33:5 says that has happened. The hiding of the face is therefore an enactment of the covenant curses, not a mood, and the promise of healing that follows breaks the pattern of the curse.

The Branch is called a man who will build the temple of the LORD and who will 'be a priest on His throne'. This takes the king and priest promises of Jeremiah 33:17 and 18 and joins them in one person, which later readers have seen fulfilled in Christ.

God swears by his holiness not to lie to David and compares his offspring and throne to the sun and moon. It stands behind Jeremiah's covenant argument, and its lament later in the psalm shows the exile making the promise look broken, which is exactly the despair Jeremiah 33:24 addresses.

The covenant of permanent priesthood given to Phinehas and his descendants for his zeal in atoning for Israel. It is one of the promises behind verse 18 and shows that the promise of an unfailing priesthood has roots in Israel's earliest history.

The priests of the old order were many because death interrupted them, but Jesus 'has a permanent priesthood' because he lives forever. This is the New Testament's answer to the Levitical promise of Jeremiah 33:18, and it explains how that promise stands without a succession of men.

Paul says of Israel that 'God's gifts and His call are irrevocable'. It restates, in the light of Christ, the reasoning of Jeremiah 33:24 to 26, that God does not cast off the people he has chosen, and it keeps the covenant promises tied to his character and not to Israel's record.

study.oneStory:
The Bible is the story of a God who made a good world, lost it to rebellion, and set out to win it back, and Jeremiah 33 stands at one of the darkest points of the middle of that story. The question it answers from before is whether the promises made at the beginning, to Adam and Noah in the order of creation, to Abraham in a land and a blessing, to David in a throne and to Levi in a priesthood, can survive the failure of those who received them. The answer given in prison is that they can, because they never depended on the recipients.

The covenant with day and night, verse 20, is a deliberate reach back to creation. In Genesis 1:14 the lights were set in the sky to separate day from night, and in Genesis 8:22 God promised after the flood that day and night 'shall never cease'. Jeremiah argues from that order to the stability of the covenants made later. Whoever can undo the first cannot undo the second, and no one can undo the first. The chapter thus connects the story's beginning with its most dire moment, and makes the beginning the pledge for the end.

What it sets up is the coming of a king and a priest. Ezra and Nehemiah show the city rebuilt, but no Branch arrives and the throne stays empty. The post-exilic prophets keep alive the Branch, Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12, and the long silence between the testaments is filled with that hope. Then the Gospels begin, 'the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David', Matthew 1:1, and the angel's word to Mary echoes the promise of an eternal throne, Luke 1:32 and 33. The righteous Branch has come, and he is also the priest who ever lives to intercede, Hebrews 7:25.

The end of the story is a new creation and a new Jerusalem. Revelation 21 sees the holy city 'prepared as a bride', and Isaiah 62:4 had promised that Jerusalem would no longer be called Forsaken but a bride in whom the LORD delights. In that city there is no death or mourning, and God dwells with his people. The sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom, silenced in Jeremiah's day, are heard for good. The promise the prophet made from a prison cell, to a people who said they had been rejected, is the promise the whole Bible keeps: the God who made the earth and sets the sun in its course will have his people, and he will be with them.

quiz.q: What invitation does God give Jeremiah at the start of this chapter, verses 2 to 3?

options.text: To call on Him, and He will answer and show great and unsearchable things Jeremiah does not know.
options.note: Verse 3 gives this specific invitation, grounded in God's identity as the LORD who made the earth.

options.text: To stop praying entirely since the city's fate is already sealed.
options.note: The invitation is the opposite, an active call to pray and seek unsearchable things from God.

options.text: To flee the city immediately before the siege ends.
options.note: Jeremiah remains imprisoned throughout; the invitation concerns prayer, not escape.

options.text: To perform a specific ritual sacrifice for the city's protection.
options.note: The invitation is to call on God in prayer, not to perform a ritual sacrifice.

quiz.q: What does God promise for the ruined city of Jerusalem in verses 6 to 13?

options.text: Health, healing, forgiveness of sin, and the return of joy, celebration, and ordinary life to its deserted streets.
options.note: Verses 6 to 11 describe this full restoration in vivid, concrete terms of joy and renewed daily life.

options.text: That the city would remain a permanent, uninhabited ruin.
options.note: The promise is the opposite, restoration, healing, and renewed habitation.

options.text: That only the palace, not the ordinary city, would be rebuilt.
options.note: The promise includes the whole city and surrounding countryside, not the palace alone.

options.text: That the healing would come without any forgiveness of sin.
options.note: Verse 8 explicitly includes cleansing from iniquity and forgiveness of sin as part of the promised restoration.

quiz.q: What does the righteous Branch of verses 15 to 16 do, and what name is given to Jerusalem under Him?

options.text: He administers justice and righteousness in the land, and Jerusalem is called The LORD Our Righteousness.
options.note: Verses 15 to 16 give both His work and the specific new name for the secured city.

options.text: He abolishes the Davidic line entirely to establish a new dynasty.
options.note: The Branch is explicitly said to sprout for David, continuing rather than abolishing the Davidic line.

options.text: He is given the name The LORD Our Righteousness Himself in this specific chapter.
options.note: In this chapter it is the city, Jerusalem, that receives this name; Jeremiah 23:6 gives the same name to the Branch directly.

options.text: He rules only over Israel's enemies, not over Judah itself.
options.note: The Branch's rule of justice and righteousness is specifically over the land of Judah and Jerusalem, not merely over enemy nations.

quiz.q: What guarantees the certainty of God's covenant with David and the Levites in verses 19 to 22?

options.text: It is compared to God's fixed covenant with the day and the night, unbreakable as long as day and night keep their appointed times.
options.note: Verses 20 to 21 explicitly ground the Davidic and Levitical covenant in this fixed, unbreakable natural order.

options.text: It depends entirely on the continued good behavior of David's descendants.
options.note: The guarantee is grounded in God's own fixed order of creation, not in the descendants' behavior.

options.text: It is left conditional and uncertain throughout this section.
options.note: The passage presents the covenant as certain, using the impossibility of breaking day and night as its very proof.

options.text: It rests on a majority vote among the tribes of Israel.
options.note: The guarantee comes from God's own unbreakable created order, not from any human vote or decision.

quiz.q: How does this chapter answer the people's claim that God has rejected the two families He had chosen, verses 24 to 26?

options.text: God says rejecting Israel's descendants is as impossible as breaking His covenant with the fixed order of heaven and earth, so He will restore them and show compassion.
options.note: Verses 25 to 26 directly answer the despairing claim with this specific, grounded assurance.

options.text: God confirms that He has indeed permanently rejected them.
options.note: God explicitly denies this claim, grounding His denial in the fixed order of creation itself.

options.text: God remains silent and gives no response to this claim.
options.note: Verses 25 to 26 give a direct, explicit response to the people's despairing claim.

options.text: God says the rejection applies only to the house of Israel, not the house of Judah.
options.note: The response addresses both the descendants of Jacob and of David together, not one house alone.

questions: God invited Jeremiah to call on Him and be shown great and unsearchable things, even from a prison cell. What would it look like for you to call on God expectantly in your own confined or difficult circumstances?
God promised full healing and forgiveness for a city under deserved judgment. Where do you need to receive God's forgiveness rather than continuing to carry guilt He has already promised to remove?
The city was to be renamed The LORD Our Righteousness, a righteousness not its own. Where are you relying on your own righteousness instead of resting in the righteousness Christ gives?

God grounded His unbreakable covenant in the fixed order of day and night. What circumstance in your life makes God's promises feel uncertain, and how does His own unchanging character speak to that uncertainty?
The people despaired, saying God had rejected them completely. Where have you spoken despair over your own situation that God's word actually contradicts?

translationNotes.note: Great and unsearchable things renders a Hebrew phrase suggesting fortified, inaccessible things, secrets normally hidden, which God offers to reveal to those who call on Him even in dire circumstances.

The name The LORD Our Righteousness given here to the city matches, word for word, the name given to the Branch Himself in Jeremiah 23:6, linking the security of the city inseparably to the righteousness of its coming king.

The appeal to an unbreakable covenant with the day and the night uses the most stable, observable phenomenon available to ancient hearers as proof of God's own unbreakable faithfulness to His promises.
